title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Whence uncertainty?

Unlike regression the Das Gupta method doesn’t really have a concept of an error term - all results are calculated algebraically (Das Gupta 1993)
But we might still want to quantify uncertainty in the results of a standardization and decomposition
Bootstrapping is a general purpose way to achieve this (Carsey and Harden 2014)
It can also show where results might be sensitive to small changes in the data (typically if the absolute difference between the rates you are decomposing is small) - we will see an example of this later
In this session we will introduce bootstrapping and describe the process to bootstrap a standardization and decomposition analysis

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping

Bootstrapping is a resampling method where you create an empirical distribution of estimates of your quantity of interest through resampling
It is kind of a dumb strategy - it doesn’t try to be clever and use maths to calculate the appropriate uncertainty with appeals to asymptotics, it just reshuffles your data a bunch and re-runs your analysis on each resampled dataset
The clever maths way assumes your data comes from a nice smooth distribution; bootstrapping makes an empirical distribution via resampling

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping

There are different ways to achieve this
Here we adopt a non-parametric bootstrap (Carsey and Harden 2014) where you sample with replacement from the original data and re-run the analysis on each bootstrap draw
This is also what Li (2017) does in the Stata rdecompose command
We will (briefly) introduce bootstrapping in general, and there is a worked example in the practical

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping example

In this example we want to calculate the mean and the standard error of the mean for a toy dataset


set.seed(387) # for reproducibility

results <- c(1, 3, 2.7, 10, 1)

results

[1]  1.0  3.0  2.7 10.0  1.0

mean(results)

[1] 3.5

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping example

Now we sample with replacement from the results to create a new set of results the same size as the original results


boot_1 <- sample(results, size = length(results), replace = TRUE)

data.frame(results = results, boot_1 = boot_1)

  results boot_1
1     1.0    1.0
2     3.0    1.0
3     2.7    3.0
4    10.0    1.0
5     1.0    2.7

data.frame(results = mean(results), boot_1 = mean(boot_1))

  results boot_1
1     3.5    1.7

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping example

And do it again…


boot_2 <- sample(results, size = length(results), replace = TRUE)

data.frame(results = results, boot_1 = boot_1, boot_2 = boot_2)

  results boot_1 boot_2
1     1.0    1.0      1
2     3.0    1.0      3
3     2.7    3.0      1
4    10.0    1.0      3
5     1.0    2.7      1

data.frame(results = mean(results), boot_1 = mean(boot_1), boot_2 = mean(boot_2))

  results boot_1 boot_2
1     3.5    1.7    1.8

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping example

… and again …


boot_3 <- sample(results, size = length(results), replace = TRUE)

data.frame(results = results, boot_1 = boot_1, boot_2 = boot_2, boot_3 = boot_3)

  results boot_1 boot_2 boot_3
1     1.0    1.0      1   10.0
2     3.0    1.0      3   10.0
3     2.7    3.0      1    1.0
4    10.0    1.0      3    1.0
5     1.0    2.7      1    2.7

data.frame(results = mean(results), boot_1 = mean(boot_1), boot_2 = mean(boot_2), boot_3 = mean(boot_3))

  results boot_1 boot_2 boot_3
1     3.5    1.7    1.8    4.9

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping example

… like 1000 times. Then we can see the range of results from the resampling.


boot_1000 <- sample(results, size = length(results), replace = TRUE)

data.frame(results = results, boot_1 = boot_1, boot_2 = boot_2, boot_3 = boot_3, boot_1000 = boot_1000)

  results boot_1 boot_2 boot_3 boot_1000
1     1.0    1.0      1   10.0         1
2     3.0    1.0      3   10.0         1
3     2.7    3.0      1    1.0         1
4    10.0    1.0      3    1.0        10
5     1.0    2.7      1    2.7        10

data.frame(results = mean(results), boot_1 = mean(boot_1), boot_2 = mean(boot_2), boot_3 = mean(boot_3), boot_1000 = mean(boot_1000))

  results boot_1 boot_2 boot_3 boot_1000
1     3.5    1.7    1.8    4.9       4.6

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Boostrapping example

With non-parametric bootstrapping you resample the data and then perform whatever analysis you like on each resample
You then get an empirical distribution of results (remember the histogram!)
Pros: this will (almost) always work, makes no assumptions about distributions or anything
Cons: the amount of memory required scales with the number of units, your computer might run out of memory/catch on fire - if you are analysing population level data from India this approach will take a lot longer than if you are analysing population data from Scotland
If you are planning to bootstrap some large data you will have to think about the practicalities (feel free to ask us if you are planning this!)

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping standardization and decomposition

Standardization and Decomposition often uses aggregate data
To use the non-parametric bootstrap here you need1 to expand the data out to unit-level data, then take the re-samples, then aggregate each re-sample back up to perform the standardization and decomposition

At least, I don’t know of any alternatives! And this is also what Li (2017) does. If there are other clever ways to do this let me know!

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping in practice

To do this in practice you need to create a function (in R; a ‘program’ in Stata) to essentially “uncount”/explode/expand the data into individual level data (where the number of rows = size of total population), then re-sample the unit-level data with replacement, then aggregate back up to the level of the original data
Then you standardize and decompose each resampled, aggregated dataset

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping in practice

‘Explode’ the aggregate data
Resample the exploded data say 200 times1
Aggregate each of the 200 datasets
Standardize and decompose 200 times
Summarise the results

There isn’t really a good answer for how many is ‘enough’ other than ‘it depends’. As a rule of thumb, the further into the tails you go the more draws you need to get a reliable estimate (see example on slide twenty here). People often use 1,000 but that’s just by convention

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Summarising the results

After all this you can calculate a standard error or confidence interval around the decomposition results (see Li (2017))
There are lots of ways to do this (Efron and Hastie 2016), but often people just take percentiles of the bootstrap distribution (the worst option)
Or you can visualize the empirical distribution of the results as we did before

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
A nice example

fine-fig

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
When things go wrong

Decomposition will decompose whatever difference there is - even if it is very small
The sampling distribution of underlying rates is usually quite nice (a Normal approximation is probably fine)
But a decomposition is essentially a ratio (remember the session on rates as products) - a transformation of the standardized rates

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
When things go wrong

The sampling distribution of a transformed quantity will not necessarily be the same as the sampling distribution of the two underlying quantities
In particular the sampling distribution of ratios can be nice or really not nice (Franz 2007)
(If you are not finding this very intuitive don’t worry! I didn’t either!)

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
The sampling distribution of decomposition

If there isn’t much difference in the underlying crude rate you are decomposing (in a hand-wavy way, if the difference is not statistically significant) then things can go haywire
If the standardized rates are very close together then the decomposition can involve dividing by very small numbers
Uh oh

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text: Dividing by small numbers

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Ratios of normals

If the crude rates are close together and you add some uncertainty in these rates via bootstrapping they may overlap
Because the calculations for decomposition involve division the resulting distribution of the decomposition can go haywire
Ben navigate to the ratios example
(AI again sorry)

A not-so-nice example

But if we compare 2015 and 2016…

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition

A not-so-nice example

The scale runs from -10,000% to +10,000%!
So lets zoom in for a closer look

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition

A not-so-nice example

haywire-fig

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
A not-so-nice example

The average bootstrap replication (the blue dot) does not match the observed data (the red dot)!
This isn’t a sample size problem - more bootstrap replications will give the same results
Would you be happy to present those results in a paper?

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
How can this be?

I was very confused by the bad decomposition - why would the bootstrapping lead to these wild estimates (huge confidence intervals not centered on the true values!)
The thing I was bootstrapping was the underlying data - and the bootstrapped distribution of the crude rates is fine
But the decomposition is a transformation of these rates, and the properties of the rates do not necessarily transfer downstream to the transformation

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
section: Do I need to worry about this?
text:
Do I need to worry about this?

Maybe you could argue that you don’t need to factor in uncertainty in the underlying rates - in this case we are working with adminisrative data , the reconviction cohorts are what they are etc
This is an actual philosophical debate (see Verlaan and Langton 2024)
But maybe you are working with survey data when you have a rate and a standard error
I (Ben) also think it’s useful to know how sensitive your results are to small changes in the input data, as much for pragmatic reasons as philosophical reasons
Bootstrapping the raw data (nonparametric simulation (see Carsey and Harden 2014)) can show when your results are fragile to small permutations in the data (see also Giordano, Meager, and Broderick 2026)

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Two practical suggestions

Check whether the difference in crude rates between comparator is statistically significant before you do your standardization and decomposition (just a standard prop.test() in R or prtest in Stata)
You can also bootstrap your results a few times anyway as a matter of course just to see if something breaks

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
section: Bootstrapping in practice: Exploding the data

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping: 2. Resampling

Now we have an ‘individual’ level dataset for our reconviction cohorts we can resample from them with replacement
We use functions from the {rsample} package to do this in a memory efficient way
Because bootstrapping uses random number generation we need to set the seed before starting so our results are reproducible
We also need to set the number of draws. We’ll use 200 for speed; but more is always better


library(rsample)

set.seed(12345)

n_draws <- 200

draws_2004_2016 <- 
dat_2004_2016_long |> 
  group_by(year) |> # we bootstrap within years - this keeps the sizes of the reconviction cohorts the same
  rsample::bootstraps(times = n_draws)

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping: 3. Aggregating

Now we can convert these memory-efficient, individual level resamples from our data to aggregate data ready to standardize and decompose
To do this we need to use R’s programming functions to iterate over each bootstrap resample and aggregate them
We will write a helper function to do this

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Writing an R function

Functions in R let you easily re-run code
If you have not written an R function before you might want to check out the Functions chapter in R for Data Science (Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund 2023)

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping: 3. Aggregating

Now we have our helper function we can apply it to each bootstrap draw
We use the map function from the {purrr} package
Jenny Bryan has written the definitive guide to iteration with {purrr}
The basic intuition is each bootstrap draw is a row of our draws_2004_2016 dataframe, and we want to aggregate each one
In other words, we want to map the aggregation to each of the bootstrap draws

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping: 3. Aggregating

draws_2004_2016 <- 
draws_2004_2016 |> 
 mutate(agg_data = map(splits, uncount_split))

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping: 4. Standardize and decompose

We can use the same pattern of creating a helper function and then applying it to each row of draws_2004_2016 to standardize and decompose 200 times

title: Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
Uncertainty in Standardization and Decomposition
text:
Bootstrapping: 4. Standardize and decompose

NB this might take a while!


draws_2004_2016 <- 
draws_2004_2016 |> 
  mutate(results = map(agg_data, calc_dg), # apply dgnpop to each aggregated dataset
         draw = 1:n_draws) |> # add an index which says which draw number the results are from
  select(draw, results) # only keep the draw number and results column

R examples use the DasGuptR package. We (mainly Josiah) wrote this!
Stata examples use the rdecompose command [@liRateDecompositionAggregate2017]. Seems neat!
For obvious reasons we are more familiar with the R version, and so focus on that
For some of the more complex examples we only provide R examples. You (or a friendly LLM) may be able to translate these to Stata





Or maybe not. I found that LLMs (the free ChatGPT one) was not at all good with rdecompose - perhaps because the documentation isn’t that extensive
